extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in wartime news and British politics
extracted.subtask_description: A newspaper report summarizing the two-day House of Commons debate on the Norwegian campaign, including Prime Minister Chamberlain's statement, opposition attacks, military criticism, and international reactions. Focus is on conveying speeches, criticisms, and immediate political/military consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure air bases / air superiority
rubrics_metrics.description: “Our inability to secure the air-dromes from which we could operate fighters.” (Chamberlain) — lack of adequate airdromes prevented fighter operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article repeatedly attributes the Trondheim failure to inadequate airfields and inability to prevent rapid arrival of German reinforcements; implies a prerequisite of securing usable air bases before amphibious/land operations, and the need to plan demolitions and defenses to delay enemy reinforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Command of sea power / naval cooperation
rubrics_metrics.description: “Without naval co-operation, the whole operation was doomed to failure.” (Sir Roger / critics) — naval support and control of fjords were vital to the success of operations such as taking Trondheim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics argue the Admiralty and naval staff failed to force Trondheim Fjord and that decisive use of the fleet might have brought victory; guidance emphasizes coordinated naval-land operations and giving navy authority/clear mission to support land objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate scouting and reconnaissance before landings
rubrics_metrics.description: Press and MPs 'assail lack of scouting' and note the difficulty of Namsos and Andalsnes as landing points; 'connoitering landing spots' was essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report stresses that insufficient reconnaissance of landing sites (small fishing ports with no unloading facilities) contributed to operational failure; implies pre-landing intelligence and site preparation are required for amphibious expeditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed, swiftness and vigor in action (avoid dithering)
rubrics_metrics.description: Calls for 'swiftness and vigor in action' and criticism that ministers did not act 'swiftly or consistently' in the affair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple speakers insist operations require prompt, decisive action; delays in dispatching troops or indecision (e.g., waiting for inadequate ports) are presented as operational flaws that invite failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate troop selection and training
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism that 'young boys without training had been sent to Norway' and that more experienced men should have been used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article implies that matching troop experience to mission complexity is a criterion of good conduct; deploying inadequately trained personnel for difficult campaigns is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid complacency; recognize imminent threats
rubrics_metrics.description: Warnings to 'face the facts and not hide our heads in the sand' and that 'people do not yet realize the extent or imminence of the threat.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several speakers urge realism about German capabilities and the need to abandon overoptimism; political leadership is judged on correctly assessing and communicating the threat level rather than being 'complacent' or 'overoptimistic.'

rubrics_metrics.name: National unity / whole‑hearted cooperation
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals for 'national unity', 'coalition cabinet', and 'the whole‑hearted co‑operation of employers and workers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article presents cross-party cooperation and unity of society and institutions as essential to the war effort; fragmentation and partisan attacks are framed as weakening national defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralized, effective wartime leadership (supreme war directorate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Calls for a 'supreme war directorate' and a 'really national Government' and description of Churchill given responsibility for 'supervision of military operations from day to day.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics argue for clear, centralized strategic command to coordinate military and civilian efforts; the creation of specialized wartime leadership roles (e.g., Churchill's new responsibilities) is offered as the remedy for disjointed policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability and inquiry into failures
rubrics_metrics.description: Demands for 'an inquiry' or 'a committee or commission with power to examine military and civilian officials ... to discover the cause of the setback.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPs call for formal investigations to assign responsibility and learn lessons; the article presents such inquiries as a standard response to major operational failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate anti‑aircraft and air defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions whether the Government had 'sufficient anti‑aircraft ... in Norway' and repeated emphasis on the 'importance of defenses against attacks from the air.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speakers highlight the need for adequate AA defenses and preparation against air attack; lack of such defenses is cited as a deficiency to be remedied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentrate forces; avoid dangerous dispersion
rubrics_metrics.description: Warnings that Allied forces 'must not be dispersed' and that troops sent to Norway might have been more valuable in France; Chamberlain urged not to disperse forces while preparing to deliver blows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article frames dispersion of forces across multiple fronts as strategically risky; concentration for decisive action and careful allocation of limited forces is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect supply lines and avoid loss of stores/material
rubrics_metrics.description: Admissions that 'We have lost all our supplies from Norway' and that 'loss of material was not negligible' with prospective supply insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintaining and protecting logistics and supplies is presented as critical; loss of stores and ships has strategic and prestige costs and is a metric used to judge the campaign's conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure suitable transport and landing infrastructure
rubrics_metrics.description: Description of landing points as 'small, almost fishing ports with no real facilities for unloading heavy material.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational planning should account for port and unloading capacity; choosing inadequate landing sites is highlighted as a contributing factor to failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate strategic command from divisional command
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertion that 'no man in charge of major strategy should also be in command of a division.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article records concern that conflation of strategic and tactical commands weakens leadership effectiveness; recommends role clarity and delegation to avoid overburdening strategic leaders with divisional command tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political timing of censure and pressure (parliamentary strategy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Labour decided 'not to move for a vote of censure' despite attacks, believing other tests would come later; some urged immediate motions or inquiries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece treats the decision whether to seek immediate parliamentary censure as a strategic judgment—balancing immediate political advantage versus waiting for fuller evidence or later tests; this is presented as a standard of political strategy rather than a military one.
